issues.legal_issue: A finding that the first information report was delayed and unexplained cannot sustain an acquittal when the informant gave a reason for waiting and that reason was not challenged in cross-examination.
material_facts: The informant said that no one would accompany her to the police station in the dark, so she waited until morning to report the attack.
Although she was cross-examined at length, she was not asked about the reason for the delay or challenged on her account of it.
The High Court treated the delay as unexplained.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s conclusion that the delay was unexplained was unsustainable.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the reason for the delay was stated in the report and that there was no requirement to provide further details; in any event, the stated reason was not challenged in cross-examination. No earlier case or statutory provision was relied on for this conclusion.

predicates.state_appeal_from_acquittal: The prosecution appeals against an acquittal.
predicates.informant_states_reason_for_reporting_la: The informant gives a reason for waiting before reporting the alleged offence.
predicates.reason_not_challenged_in_cross_examinati: The opposing party does not question or challenge the informant about that reason during cross-examination.

issues.definition: When the prosecution appeals an acquittal, an unexplained-delay finding is unsustainable if the informant gave a reason for reporting later and that reason was not challenged in cross-examination.

issues.legal_issue: The prosecution need not explain injuries on an accused as having been inflicted by the deceased when the accused do not claim that the deceased caused them.
material_facts: The accused did not claim, including in their examination under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, that the deceased had inflicted their injuries.
Their account was that unidentified assailants caused their injuries while they tried to intervene.
They did not report those injuries to the police.
The High Court relied on the prosecution’s failure to explain the injuries.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s reliance on the non-explanation of the accused persons’ injuries was unsustainable.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the distinction between injuries alleged to have been caused by the deceased and injuries which the accused attributed to unidentified assailants; because the accused did not claim that the deceased caused their injuries, an explanation on that basis did not arise. The Court referred to the accused’s examination under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. No earlier case was relied on.

predicates.state_appeal_from_acquittal: The prosecution appeals against an acquittal.
predicates.accused_do_not_attribute_injuries_to_dec: The accused do not claim that the deceased inflicted their injuries.
predicates.accused_attribute_injuries_to_unknown_as: The accused attribute their injuries to unidentified assailants.

issues.definition: When the prosecution appeals an acquittal, the prosecution need not explain the accused persons’ injuries as having been caused by the deceased if the accused deny that attribution and instead blame unidentified assailants.

issues.legal_issue: The absence of a visible blood trail does not by itself undermine the prosecution account when the body was dragged and blood-stained earth was recovered at the scene or nearby.
material_facts: The informant said the accused dragged the deceased’s body to another house.
The trial court considered that dragging the body could stain the accused persons’ clothes rather than leave a trail of blood.
The investigating officer testified that he collected blood-stained earth from several places.
The High Court did not explain why it disagreed with the trial court’s assessment.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s treatment of the absence of a blood trail was unsustainable.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed the alleged absence of a blood trail in light of the evidence that the body was dragged and that blood-stained earth was collected at several places; it noted that the case therefore did not involve an absence of blood at the occurrence site or nearby. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on.

predicates.state_appeal_from_acquittal: The prosecution appeals against an acquittal.
predicates.body_dragged_from_occurrence_site: The evidence is that the body was dragged from the place of occurrence.
predicates.blood_stained_earth_recovered_nearby: The investigating officer recovers blood-stained earth at the occurrence site or nearby.

issues.definition: When the prosecution appeals an acquittal, the absence of a visible blood trail does not undermine the prosecution account if the body was dragged and blood-stained earth was recovered at or near the scene.

issues.legal_issue: An acquittal cannot stand when its stated grounds are unsustainable in light of the evidence supporting the trial court’s conviction.
material_facts: The trial court convicted the accused based principally on the eyewitness account, which remained unshaken despite lengthy cross-examination.
The prosecution also established recovery of weapons at the accused persons’ instance.
The High Court acquitted the accused on grounds concerning reporting delay, injuries to the accused, and the absence of a blood trail.
The Supreme Court found the High Court’s conclusions on those grounds unsustainable.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court set aside the acquittal and restored the trial court’s order of conviction and sentence.
issues.legal_principle: The Court concluded on the evidence before it that the grounds on which the High Court set aside the convictions were unsustainable and that the trial court’s order should be restored. No earlier case or specific statutory provision was relied on for this appellate conclusion.
